title: Flint and Alba Save the Light
markdown:
The Great Lantern of Port Blossom kept a golden eye on Mariner’s Bay. Most evenings it turned as steadily as a heartbeat. Ships trusted that blink. Then one foggy night the pattern broke. The beam stuttered, coughed, and went thin. Mist swallowed the horizon. Hulls out there had only guesswork left.

“The turning part is jammed,” cried Alba, a lighthouse gull with pearl-white feathers. “The ships will be lost.”

Flint the ferret popped from a coil of rope, whiskers fizzing. “Lost? Not on my watch. What’s amiss?”

“The lamp room. Now.”

That was the first crisis: the climb. The path up the rock was a dragon’s spine, wet and mean. Wind shoved. Alba soared, a pale scrap of certainty. Flint scrambled, sandy fur, claws hunting tiny holds. A step slid. He hung by two toes until Alba’s call found him a better crack. “Left. The dark wet one. Not the shiny liar.”

He gained the opening and paused just long enough to taste salt and oil. The bay below was a blank page. Then he darted in.

The Great Lantern pulsed like a tired heart. A stone, big as Flint’s head, sat wedged in the gears. That was the second crisis: the jam itself. Flint shoved. The stone stayed. Alba landed and set her beak to the same stubborn rock. They pushed together. Metal groaned. The stone only settled deeper, as if it liked the view.

They stopped. Flint’s paws shook. Alba’s feathers stood in the draught. If they broke a gear, the light would die for good. If they did nothing, the light was already dying.

The third crisis arrived as a sound: a ship’s bell, too close, lost in the soup. The lantern’s weak blink caught a mast and lost it again. Time had run out of polite options.

“Together,” Flint said. “On three. Not pretty. True.”

They heaved. Alba’s beak found a chip Flint’s paws could not. Flint’s shoulder found a give Alba’s beak could not. The stone screamed against brass and tumbled free, a dull thud on the lamp-room floor.

The Great Lantern took a breath and became a sword of gold. Blink, blink, blink — the old rhythm, the one the charts knew. Fog tore like a shy curtain. The near ship found the channel and came in with all its paint still on.

Alba’s voice went quiet. “They’ll be safe.”

Flint sat on the stone that had tried to steal the night, chest puffed once, then ordinary again. “Paws and a beak. That will do.”

Below, Port Blossom’s windows remembered how to look golden. The lantern turned. The bay, for one more night, had an eye.
